title: Pitching
brief_markdown:
Everything from Modules 2 to 6 gets spent in this meeting. Module 2 told you what to say, Module 3 gave you the deck and the demo skeleton, Modules 4 to 6 put a qualified Head of E-commerce on your calendar. Now you have twenty minutes with him and his TikTok Shop manager, and the only output that counts is a next step with a date on it.

### What a pitch has to do
By the end of the call three things have to be true in the buyer's head: the problem is big enough to fix now, Myda fixes it, and *his* team would actually capture the value. Think of it as a product: size of the pain × how well he understood you × how much he believes it will work for him. The right accounts raise the first term (Module 4), presenting as a conversation raises the second, a demo on his own creators' videos raises the third. Every buyer discounts your claims by his doubt; his own videos are what shrink the discount. In twenty minutes you will not close; the goal is a scoped pilot. And if it is clearly not going to happen, find that out on the call, not over three weeks of chasing.

### Before the call: fifteen minutes, not optional
Block 15 minutes before every pitch and 30 after it, so follow-up happens while the call is warm. In the fifteen, get into your head: the signals of pain (affiliate creators, videos a month on their TikTok Shop, which creators repeat), the size of the prize (one brand, or twelve agency clients), what they pay today (a UGC retainer, a creator tool, nothing), who is on the call and who sits above them (Marcus's CMO), and who would use Myda day to day. Then the Module 3 customisation: three of their own creators' videos run through Myda, one hit and two misses, feedback saved offline in case the wifi dies. Note the known unknowns; those are your discovery questions. Write the goal of the call in one sentence: with Marcus and his manager, a scoped pilot; with someone below the decision maker, the second meeting with the person who signs. Stand up for the call.

### Opening and agenda
Two minutes of rapport, no more, then cross to business through the professional side ("how long have you been running the affiliate programme?"). Then the time check and the agenda, phrased as a small contract: "We have twenty minutes. I'd like to ask a few questions about how creator videos get reviewed today, show you Myda on three of your own creators' videos, and if it makes sense, agree what a pilot would look like. Does that work?" A buyer who agrees to the agenda has agreed to the ending.

### Discovery: the five minutes founders skip
Five minutes of questions decide whether the next fifteen are tailored or wasted. You need the pain and how badly it hurts, how it is solved today and why that fails, who would use Myda, who decides, how they have bought tools before, and timing. The classic budget-authority-need-timeline test is too strict for a category the buyer did not know existed last month; nobody has a line item for "AI creator feedback". Test the size of the pain and the urgency instead, and whether they have ever paid to solve it: the $6k retainer tells you Marcus has a buying process. Lead with what you found: not "do you work with creators?" but "you've got about 150 affiliates and TikTok is roughly a third of DTC. When a video misses the brief, who tells the creator, and how long does that take?" Then cascade: how it is handled today, what that costs, what happens if it stays like this through Q4. Tie questions to what Myda does: "when a video hits, can you say why?" Write every answer down; you will quote it back within ten minutes. If the pain is not there, say so and give him his time back. The rule for stopping: you can state his problem in his words, you know who would use it, who decides, what they pay today, and what "it worked" would mean to him. Then pitch; anything else, ask when the relevant slide comes up.

### Presenting as a conversation
The deck sets the mental model: the pain, why the Slack channel and the agency fail, how Myda works, proof. It is not a feature tour. Skip every slide he already agreed with in discovery and say so: "as you said, your manager reviews every affiliate video on her phone at night, so I'll skip this one." Jump to an appendix slide when a question lands and come back. Repeat the two or three points you want him to carry out of the room, and check he is following with specific questions, never "does that make sense?", which only invites a polite yes: "is that how it goes with your affiliates? It's fine if it isn't." Each yes, to the pain, to the failure of the current fix, to the fit, is a point scored toward the close. Slow down; nerves and familiarity both make you speed up.

### The demo on his videos
The deck made promises; the demo proves them while you both look at the same screen. Use his creators' videos, pulled before the call. If you hear yourself say "imagine if", you have a data problem. Order the three value buckets from the Module 3 skeleton by what discovery said matters to him, and cut the one that does not. Pause after each and ask the user on the call, not the buyer: "would you have told the creator the same thing?", "what would you have done with this on Tuesday?" Speak each person's language: the TikTok Shop manager cares about her evenings and her creators not hating her; Marcus cares about GMV per video and the retainer.

### Proof, then price
After the demo, back to slides for proof, in metrics he already tracks: minutes of feedback per video, round-two hook rate, approved videos a week. No numbers yet means "here is what the beta measures", never an invented figure. If he asks the price now, good: that is a buying signal. Flip to the pricing slide, state the price against the comparable he named ("less than a fifth of the retainer"), then stop talking and wait. If he does not ask, trial-close: "given all this, is it something you'd see fixing the hit-or-miss problem?" Then ask: "is there anything stopping us from starting a pilot next week?"

### Objections are the work
A no at this point is usually a "not sure, because". Catch it, find the question under the question, answer with his numbers and a slide, check that it landed, return to the ask. The generic buckets: no authority (he is sold, so you run point on the CMO meeting and book it now); no need (restate the signals you found and ask what you missed; a squishy answer hides a different objection); happy as we are (make the cost of the status quo visible in his numbers); "not mid-Q4" (make it easy: his creators already live in Discord, nothing changes; or sign now, start in January); price (ask how far apart you are: ten percent is a discount, fifty is a value conversation); no budget (it exists, it is called the retainer); "can we trial it" (that means "I need more proof": ask what proof, offer a guided session, never hand out logins with no structure). Myda-specific ones (ChatGPT, the agency, who sees the videos, "we're too small") get one answer each, with proof. Anything heard twice becomes an appendix slide.

### Leaving the call
Summarise what he agreed to, in his words. Propose the pilot with scope (which creators, how many videos, how many weeks), the success metric, the owner on his side and the start date. Book the next call before anyone hangs up; "let's touch base in a month" becomes a dated invite with an agenda. Within two hours, in the same thread, send what was agreed, who does what by when, and the send-deck. Then log it.

### This week
Run the pre-call checklist on your next two booked calls, each of you. Write the discovery bank together and read it aloud until the questions sound like yours. Rehearse the objection map out loud, taking turns as Marcus.

### What you build in this module
The pitch and demo runbook: pre-call checklist with owners and timing, opening and agenda script, discovery banks for agencies and brands with the rule for when to stop, the slide-by-slide guide to presenting as a conversation, the demo flow on the prospect's own videos with pause points, the objection map for everything Dana, Marcus and Sofia say, the close of the meeting, the two-hour follow-up email and what gets logged. It consumes the `company` narrative and the `materials` deck and demo skeleton; it does not rewrite them.

**Drill:** Marcus, 20-minute video call with his TikTok Shop manager listening; goal a scoped pilot with an owner and a start date, next call booked before he leaves.

build.spec_markdown:
Produce {{company}}'s pitch and demo runbook, section by section, in this order. Work one question at a time; record each section with update_artifact as soon as it is good enough, then move to the next. Pull the problem, who has it, cost, alternatives and price from the `company` and `pricing` artifacts, and the deck outline, send-deck, demo skeleton (three value buckets, workday story, pre-call customisation checklist) and FAQ answers from the `materials` artifact. Reference those by section; do not rewrite them here. The runbook is the document either founder opens fifteen minutes before a pitch.

1. **Pre-call prep checklist.** A table: item, owner (the founder running the call or the other one), when (T-24h or T-15min), done-when. Mandatory rows: research (the prospect's TikTok Shop footprint: number of affiliate creators, videos per month, categories, markets; what they pay today for this: UGC agency, creator-management tool, nothing; who sits above the contact and who would use {{company}} day to day); which creator videos to pull (the rule: three videos from the prospect's own affiliates, one that hit and two that missed, run through {{company}} before the call, feedback screenshots saved offline); who is on the call and what each person cares about (user, first-line manager, CXO: one line of language for each); known unknowns to ask in discovery; the stated goal for this call in one sentence (scoped pilot, second meeting with the decision maker, or disqualify); the rapport hook; tooling (screen share tested, offline copies, notebook open, 30-minute block after the call for follow-up).
2. **Opening and agenda script.** Two minutes of rapport with the transition line to business, then the time check and the agenda as a micro-contract in {{company}}'s words: what you will do, why it helps them, how long, ending with a question that asks for agreement. Under 60 words. Plus the one-line disqualification exit for a call that discovery kills, phrased as respect for their time.
3. **Discovery question bank.** Two tables: agencies (Dana's world) and brands (Marcus's and Sofia's). At least eight questions each, ordered pain → how it is solved today → cost → who would use it → who decides and how they have bought before → timing. Columns: the question (leading, built on what research found: "you've got about 150 affiliates and TikTok is a third of DTC..." not "do you work with creators?"), what a good answer reveals, what disqualifies. Then the rule for when to stop discovering and start pitching, written as the five things you must be able to say before you open the deck; everything else becomes rolling discovery on the relevant slide.
4. **Presenting the deck as a conversation.** A table over the main-deck slides from `materials` §1: slide, skip when (which discovery answer makes it redundant, and the sentence that says so), double down when, the validation question to ask on it (specific, never "does that make sense?"), and the appendix slide to jump to if a given question lands. Plus the three points to repeat throughout the call.
5. **Demo flow on the prospect's own videos.** Ordered by the three value buckets from `materials` §5, with the rule for reordering from discovery and which bucket to cut when time runs short. For each bucket: what to show on their videos, the pause point, the question for the user on the call (TikTok Shop manager or content person) and the question for the decision maker, and the proof slide to flip back to afterwards. Then the never-list: no "imagine if", no generic demo account when their videos exist, no feature that is not tied to a discovery answer.
6. **Proof and price moment.** The switch back to proof slides after the demo (which metrics, in their units, or "what the beta measures"); the trial-close question; how to state the price against the comparable the prospect named, then stop talking; the direct ask for the pilot.
7. **Objection-handling map.** One row per objection. Mandatory: every objection in the three persona files — Dana: "we're pretty happy with our process", "send me something", "is it free?", "how is this different from just using ChatGPT?"; Marcus: "we have an agency for this", "my team can do this with ChatGPT", "show me the data", "I'm not switching workflows mid-Q4", "why now?", "who else uses this?", "what does it cost?"; Sofia: "is it free during beta?", "we're really small, is this for us?", "can my content person just use it without me?", "what happens to our creators' videos, do you train on them?" — plus the generic ones: "I need to run this past my CMO / co-founder", "let's touch base in a month", "can we just get a trial login?", "no budget this quarter", "that's expensive". Columns: the objection as they say it, the question under the question, the acknowledge-then-reframe answer in two sentences (grant the alternative its strength first), the proof to show (slide, screenshot, number, or `TODO: measure in beta`), and the question that returns to the ask. Flag any objection heard twice in the CRM log for an appendix slide.
8. **Close of the meeting.** The summary script in the prospect's words; the pilot proposal with scope (which creators, how many videos, how many weeks), success metric, owner on their side and start date; the next-step booking before leaving the call, including the response to "let's touch base later" (a dated invite with an agenda, set on the call); and what you say when the answer is a clear no.
9. **Follow-up email within two hours.** Template, sent in the same thread as the invite: what was agreed in their words, who does what by when, the send-deck attached, exactly one call to action. Under 150 words.
10. **What is logged.** The CRM row after every pitch: stage reached, key quotes, objections heard, pilot scope proposed, next step with date; plus any discovery question that did not work and any objection the map could not answer, so the runbook and the deck appendix get updated.

Standards to enforce on every section: every question and answer is in the prospect's language and would make Dana or Marcus say "that's me"; every objection answer grants the alternative its strength before naming the gap; no number appears that {{company}} has not measured (write `TODO: measure in beta`); the agenda and the close are micro-contracts (what, why, agree?). Push back on "does that make sense?" questions, on a demo plan that does not start from the prospect's own videos, on objection answers longer than two sentences, and on close scripts that end with "let me know what you think". Mark the artifact done only when all ten sections exist and both founders could run tomorrow's pitch from it without the deck notes.

drill.scenario: The pitch meeting Marcus agreed to after the Module 3 email thread. Twenty minutes booked on video, hard stop. His TikTok Shop manager, Priya, is on the call: she reviews the affiliate videos herself and has been told to judge whether {{company}}'s feedback is any good. Marcus has looked at the site and the send-deck and expects a demo; he respects a seller who sets an agenda and asks first, and interrupts one who reads slides. You pulled three of his affiliates' videos before the call (say which and what {{company}} said about them). He will test 'we have an agency for this', 'my team can do this with ChatGPT' and 'what does it cost', and if you drift, 'I'm not switching workflows mid-Q4'. Your goal: a scoped pilot with a success metric, an owner on his side and a start date, and the next call booked before he leaves.
drill.buyer_opening: Right, we've got twenty minutes and I've got a hard stop. This is Priya, she runs our TikTok Shop and actually looks at the videos, so she'll tell me if this is any good. I've seen the site and the deck. Show me what it actually does.

rows.criterion: Set the agenda as a micro-contract (what, why, time check) and got Marcus's agreement before starting discovery
Ran discovery before pitching: at least three leading questions built on research (pain, who would use it, who decides or what they pay today), and stopped when he could state the problem
Pitched the problem back in Marcus's own words, skipped what he had already agreed to, and validated with specific questions rather than 'does that make sense?'
Demoed on his own creators' videos pulled before the call, paused after each bucket with a question to Priya or Marcus, no 'imagine if' and no generic walkthrough
Switched to proof after the demo: a proof point relevant to a supplements brand on TikTok Shop in metrics he tracks, or an honest 'this is what the beta measures', no invented number
Handled the agency, ChatGPT or mid-Q4 objection with the loop: caught it, found the question under it, answered in Marcus's numbers without trashing the alternative, checked, returned to the ask
Stated the price when asked, framed against the retainer, then stopped talking: no flinch, no discount
Asked for the pilot with scope, metric, owner and start date, booked the next step before the call ended, and got a yes or a clear no

rubric.below_threshold_note: Below 10: fix the weakest section of the pitch runbook (discovery bank, demo flow or objection map) before repeating with the same persona. Carry forward the weakest row as the standing fix; add every objection Marcus raised that the map could not answer, and every discovery question that did not land, to the runbook.
